items.q: OAuth 2.x: what are the roles, modern flows, and flows to avoid?
items.a:
**Roles:** the [[b:resource owner]] grants access; the [[b:client]] requests it; the [[b:authorization server]] authenticates/authorizes and issues tokens; the [[b:resource server]] enforces the token for its API. OAuth is delegated [[g:authorization]], not a user-authentication protocol; OpenID Connect adds that layer.

Choose a flow from the client and user context:

- **Authorization Code + PKCE** for browser, native, and other user-facing clients. A server-side BFF can keep tokens away from browser JavaScript; a pure SPA remains a public client.
- **Client Credentials** when a confidential workload acts as itself, not as a user. Prefer workload identity, private-key authentication, or federation over a long-lived shared secret.
- **Device Authorization Grant** for input-constrained devices when supported.
- **Refresh Token Grant** renews an existing authorization; issuance is optional and requires replay protection.
- Avoid **Implicit** and **Resource Owner Password Credentials**. RFC 9700 recommends authorization-code responses and removes password handling from clients.

:::deep
OAuth 2.1 is still an [[o:Internet-Draft (draft-15 as reviewed in 2026)]], not an RFC. Use RFC 9700, the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, as normative deployed guidance and track the draft for consolidation changes.

Scopes and audiences must be least-privilege and resource-specific. Client Credentials must not manufacture end-user identity; when service A calls B on behalf of a user, use an explicit delegation/token-exchange design with downscoped audience rather than blindly forwarding the original token.

Passkeys/WebAuthn and MFA are authentication methods at the authorization server/identity provider, not OAuth grants. They strengthen how the user signs in while OAuth/OIDC governs tokens and delegation.
:::

items.q: How does Authorization Code + PKCE work, and why is PKCE needed?
items.a:
The client creates a high-entropy `code_verifier`, derives an S256 `code_challenge`, stores verifier plus transaction state, and redirects the browser to the authorization endpoint. After authentication/consent, the authorization server sends a short-lived, one-time code to an exactly registered redirect URI. The client redeems that code over the token endpoint and proves possession of the verifier. 
# authorization request (line breaks only for readability)
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=web&
    code_challenge=BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))&code_challenge_method=S256&
    state=BOUND_TO_BROWSER_SESSION&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example%2Fcallback
    
# back-channel token request: the stolen code is useless without verifier
POST /token
grant_type=authorization_code&code=ONE_TIME_CODE&code_verifier=ORIGINAL_VERIFIER
PKCE prevents authorization-code interception and injection. RFC 9700 requires PKCE protection for public clients; confidential clients should also use it as defense in depth. The current OAuth 2.1 draft makes PKCE part of the default authorization-code flow, but OAuth 2.1 is [[r:not yet an RFC]]. :::deep PKCE is one control in a transaction-bound flow: - use S256, high verifier entropy, one-time codes, short code lifetime, and exact redirect-URI matching; - bind `state` to the user-agent session for request/response correlation and CSRF defense; in OIDC also validate `nonce` in the ID token and the authorization-response issuer where applicable; - at token validation, check issuer and audience so a code/token from another authorization server or resource cannot be substituted; - do not put access tokens in redirect URLs. For browser apps, prefer a BFF when the deployment can support one: the BFF is the confidential OAuth client, stores tokens server-side, and exposes a Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite session cookie with CSRF protection. A pure SPA uses Authorization Code + PKCE, minimizes token lifetime/storage, enforces a strong CSP, and assumes XSS can act with any token JavaScript can access. :::

items.q: What's the difference between OAuth2 and OIDC?
items.a:
OAuth2OIDC
Answers'what is the app allowed to do''who is the user'
TokenAccess Token+ ID Token (JWT, `sub`, claims)
Purposeauthorizationauthentication (+ authorization)
OIDC is built on top of OAuth2, adding the ID Token + the `/userinfo` endpoint. Modern SSO uses OIDC. :::deep - OAuth2 returns an *access token* (what the app is allowed to do) — it does NOT standardize saying who the user is - OIDC adds the ID Token (JWT: `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `email`, `auth_time`), `/userinfo`, discovery via `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, and JWKS [[r:Common mistake]]: using the *access token* to determine user identity (wrong — the access token is for the resource server); using the ID token to call an API (wrong — the ID token is for the client to know who the user is). OTA: OIDC for B2C login (via Google/social IdP), access tokens for calling internal services with the appropriate scope. :::

items.q: What is the JWT structure, and how is it signed and verified?
items.a:
A commonly used signed JWT is the compact JWS form `header.payload.signature`, with each part base64url-encoded. The payload is [[r:not encrypted]] unless a separate JWE design is used. - Header: a pinned `alg`, a rotation key ID `kid`, and an explicit `typ` such as the access-token profile expected by the API. - Claims: `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, optionally `nbf`/`jti`, and authorization data such as scopes. - Signature: integrity/authenticity over the encoded header and payload using a trusted key. 
// Validation order; use a maintained JOSE/OAuth library, not home-grown crypto
requireExpectedTypAndAllowedAlgorithm(header);
Key key = trustedJwks.resolve(header.kid());
Claims c = jws.verifyThenDecode(key);
requireIssuer(c, EXPECTED_ISSUER);
requireAudience(c, THIS_API);
requireTimeWindow(c.nbf(), c.exp(), ALLOWED_CLOCK_SKEW);
requireScopesAndSubjectPolicy(c);
:::warn Parsing is not validation Do not authorize from unverified claims. Reject `alg: none`, algorithm/key-type confusion, unexpected `typ`, untrusted `jku`/`x5u`, missing issuer/audience/time claims, and tokens intended for another API or token class. An ID token is not an API access token. ::: :::deep JWKS handling is production logic: fetch only from issuer configuration you trust; cache keys; rate-limit refresh on an unknown `kid`; retain previous keys through the maximum token lifetime; and overlap old/new signing keys during rotation. A naïve “refetch on every unknown kid” path is a denial-of-service vector, while a cache that never refreshes breaks rotation. `typ`, issuer, audience, key set, and validation rules together prevent cross-JWT and token-substitution attacks. Signature validity says who signed bytes; authorization still has to check tenant, subject, scope/role, resource ownership, and current policy. Keep claims minimal, never put secrets in a readable payload, never log the token, and choose access-token lifetime from replay risk and revocation capability rather than a universal number of minutes. :::

items.q: JWT (stateless) vs opaque token / session — what are the trade-offs?
items.a:
JWTOpaque + introspectionSession
Validatelocally (no call to the AS)asks the AS every timeserver-side state
Revokehard (still valid until it expires)immediateeasy
Scalegood, low latencyextra round-tripneeds sticky/shared store
:::tip Bottom line JWT trades revocability for scale. Fintech typically uses: short-lived JWT access token + revocable refresh token + blacklist/rotation. ::: :::deep - need immediate revocation (locking a fraudulent account) → short-lived access token + introspection for sensitive operations, or an opaque token - [[g:common hybrid pattern]]: JWT access token for 5–15 minutes (validated locally) + server-side refresh token *rotation* (revocable, reuse detection → revokes the whole family) + `jti` denylist for emergencies 'JWT trades revocability for statelessness/scale; we compensate with a short TTL + revocation at the refresh layer' — [[r:avoid saying 'JWT is always better than sessions']]. :::

items.q: Access token vs refresh token, and what's the revocation strategy?
items.a:
- An [[b:access token]] is presented to a resource server and should be audience-restricted, least-privilege, and short enough for the replay/revocation risk. - A [[b:refresh token]] is a higher-value credential used only at the authorization server. Issuance and lifetime are policy decisions; inactivity, consent, credential, device, or risk changes can terminate the grant early. For public clients, RFC 9700 requires refresh tokens to be [[g:sender-constrained]] (for example DPoP) or rotated with reuse detection. Rotation issues a new token on every refresh, invalidates the predecessor, and revokes the active family when reuse reveals likely theft. Confidential clients must authenticate and the server must bind the token to that client. Storage follows the platform threat model: a BFF keeps OAuth tokens server-side and uses a Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookie plus CSRF defense; native apps use OS-protected storage; browser-only apps minimize token lifetime and commonly keep access tokens in memory. HttpOnly prevents JavaScript reads, not requests made by an XSS payload, so CSP and output safety still matter. **The two credentials side by side, because almost every mistake here is treating them alike:**
Access tokenRefresh token
Presented toevery resource serverthe authorization server only, never an API
Typical lifetime5–15 minuteshours to months, bounded by inactivity as well as absolute age
Blast radius if stolenbounded by the expiry you chosea standing ability to mint access tokens
Validationlocal signature check, or introspection when central revocation matters more than latencyalways a server-side lookup — it has state
Revocationusually just expiry; that is the trade a short lifetime pays forimmediate, and it takes the whole family with it
Storagememory in a browser app, OS keystore on nativenever in a browser app without a BFF holding it server-side
**Rotation with reuse detection, in the order the checks must happen:** 
// 1. the refresh arrives; look it up by its family, not just by its value
Family family = store.byToken(presented);
if (family == null) throw new InvalidGrant();
//
// 2. THE detection: this token was already spent. Only two things explain that —
//    a stolen copy being replayed, or a client that retried. Both are handled the
//    same way, because you cannot tell them apart and only one is safe to assume.
if (presented.isSuperseded()) {
    store.revokeFamily(family.id());     // kill every descendant, not just this one
    audit.refreshReuse(family.subject(), family.id());
    throw new InvalidGrant();
}
//
// 3. only now issue the pair, and mark the predecessor spent in the same write
return store.rotate(family, presented);
:::warn The retry that looks exactly like theft A client that loses the response to a refresh will retry with the old token and trip reuse detection — the user is logged out for a network blip. Absorb it at the client (one in-flight refresh per app, shared by every waiting request), not by weakening the check on the server. ::: :::deep Revocation is layered: - revoke the authorization/refresh-token family on logout, consent withdrawal, account compromise, credential reset, or reuse detection; - use opaque access tokens with introspection when immediate central revocation outweighs the availability/latency cost, or a short-lived signed token when local validation is the better trade-off; - use a `jti` denylist only for bounded emergency cases with an explicit retention/availability design; - require reauthentication or step-up with WebAuthn/MFA for high-risk operations, even when a token is valid; - consider DPoP or mTLS sender-constrained access tokens where bearer-token replay is a material risk. Never log tokens or URLs/headers containing them. Redact at ingestion, restrict security-log access, and alert on refresh reuse without recording the credential itself (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). :::

items.q: Where should a browser store JWTs: cookies, sessionStorage, or localStorage?
items.a:
**The default answer is none of those places for the JWT itself.** JWT is only a token format. Storage depends on whether it is an access, refresh or ID token and whether browser JavaScript must ever possess it. For a first-party web application with a backend, prefer a [[g:Backend for Frontend (BFF)]]. The BFF keeps OAuth access and refresh tokens server-side. The browser receives an opaque, random session identifier in a hardened cookie—not the JWT.
PlaceXSS consequenceCSRF consequenceLifetimeVerdict
BFF + HttpOnly cookiescript cannot read the cookie
but can make authenticated same-origin calls		browser sends cookie automatically
needs CSRF defense		cookie + server session policypreferred when a backend is available
Memoryrunning malicious script can request or use a token
persistent theft is harder		Authorization header is not automaticlost on reload/tab closebest direct-SPA baseline
sessionStoragesame-origin script can read and exfiltrate itnot sent automaticallyone tab; survives reloadshorter exposure, not XSS-safe
localStoragesame-origin script can read every persisted tokennot sent automaticallypersists across restarts and tabsavoid for credentials
JS-readable cookiereadable like Web Storagealso sent automatically to matching requestscookie expiryworst properties combined; do not use
**A hardened session cookie looks like this:** 
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=RANDOM_OPAQUE_ID; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Cache-Control: no-store
- HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie; it does not stop XSS from operating the application through the victim's browser. - Secure restricts transport to HTTPS. The __Host- prefix also requires Path=/ and no Domain, preventing broad subdomain scope. - Choose SameSite=Strict or Lax from the navigation flow. SameSite is defense in depth, not a universal replacement for a CSRF token, Origin/Fetch-Metadata checks and correct non-mutating GET semantics. - Rotate the session identifier on login and privilege change; enforce idle and absolute expiry server-side. Logout deletes server session state, clears the cookie and revokes the refresh-token family where supported. **What if the product is a pure SPA that calls an API directly?** Use Authorization Code + PKCE. Keep a short-lived, narrowly scoped access token in memory or an isolated service worker. Send it in Authorization: Bearer. Accept that reload loses it and re-establish authorization through the IdP session. A service worker can reduce direct token exfiltration only if it never returns tokens to the page or persists them in storage shared with the window. An XSS payload can still ask that trusted component to make allowed calls while it is running; isolation is not an XSS cure. If the authorization server issues refresh tokens to a public browser client, use rotation or sender-constrained tokens when supported, detect reuse, cap absolute lifetime and avoid persistent JavaScript-readable storage. A stolen bearer token remains usable by whoever holds it until expiry or revocation policy intervenes (13-security-oauth2.jwt-tokens.q3). **Token type matters:** - **Access token:** API credential. Keep it short-lived and out of URLs, logs, analytics and crash reports. - **Refresh token:** long-lived authority to mint access tokens. Keep it server-side whenever possible; it deserves stronger protection than the access token. - **ID token:** a client authentication result, not an API credential. Validate it during the OIDC flow, derive the local session and do not persist it merely to display profile fields. :::warn Encryption in localStorage does not close the boundary If JavaScript can decrypt the token, injected JavaScript can call the same decrypt path or use the token through your code. Moving the encryption key into the same origin only rearranges the secret. ::: :::tip Decision rule Have a backend? Use BFF plus an opaque HttpOnly cookie. Pure SPA? Prefer memory/service-worker isolation and short-lived access tokens. sessionStorage is a bounded compromise; localStorage is for non-sensitive UI state, not bearer credentials. ::: :::deep - Cookie size and transport matter: a JWT in a cookie may approach browser limits and is attached to every matching request. An opaque session id is smaller and gives logout/revocation one server-side control point. - Cookie authentication changes the API threat model from header-bearer handling to ambient authority. CORS does not replace CSRF protection; CORS governs response access, while a forged request can still have effects. - CSP, Trusted Types, dependency control and output encoding reduce XSS likelihood. None converts JavaScript-readable storage into a protected credential vault. - Do not copy this browser decision to native mobile. Native apps use the operating system's protected credential storage and an external user-agent flow (RFC 8252). - The normative source for this whole decision is the IETF BCP draft *OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications* (`draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps`). - It is still an Internet-Draft in the RFC Editor queue with no RFC number assigned, so quote it as a draft and re-check its status before calling it settled. :::

items.q: How would you design the authentication/authorization system for microservices (SSO + gateway)?
items.a:
Design three identities separately: the human/session, the OAuth client, and the calling workload.

- A central [[b:authorization server/IdP]] handles OIDC login, WebAuthn/passkeys/MFA, consent, token issuance, keys, and session risk.
- A [[b:gateway or BFF]] validates the external protocol at the edge, strips any client-supplied identity headers, and creates trusted internal context. A BFF keeps browser tokens server-side.
- Each [[b:resource-owning service]] enforces scopes plus domain authorization such as tenant, object ownership, amount, and state transition. Edge validation alone cannot decide those invariants.
- Workloads authenticate with short-lived federated identity, mTLS/SPIFFE, or an OAuth confidential-client method; avoid one shared static credential across services.

:::tip Choose one internal token contract
Either services validate an externally issued token with the exact issuer/audience profile, or a trusted edge exchanges it for a short-lived, downscoped internal token.
:::

Do not forward arbitrary identity headers or every original bearer token through all hops. Preserve the actor/delegation chain explicitly when a service acts for a user.
:::deep
Validation and authorization belong at different boundaries. The gateway can reject malformed/expired tokens, enforce coarse scopes, rate-limit, and translate protocols. The ledger still verifies that this subject may move money from this account and requires step-up for a high-risk action.

For local JWT validation, distribute trust through OIDC discovery/JWKS with bounded caches and rotation overlap. For opaque tokens, design introspection availability, caching, and revocation semantics.

Internal calls need workload identity even when user context is present; one credential answers “which service?”, the delegated token answers “for which actor and authority?”

Propagate an absolute deadline, trace context, and only the minimum identity attributes. Log authorization decisions and policy version without logging credentials or sensitive claims.
:::

items.q: What is mTLS, and how is it used for service-to-service authentication?
items.a:
[[g:mTLS]] authenticates both TLS peers with certificates while encrypting the channel. It proves possession of a private key bound to an accepted certificate/trust domain; it does not by itself decide whether that workload may perform a business action.

Common uses:

- workload-to-workload identity with certificates/SVIDs rotated by a mesh, workload-identity platform, or PKI automation;
- OAuth client authentication and certificate-bound access tokens under RFC 8705, reducing replay from a different TLS client;
- B2B partner APIs where both organizations can operate certificate issuance, renewal, revocation, and incident procedures.

DPoP (RFC 9449) is an application-layer proof-of-possession option that can sender-constrain tokens without requiring the same TLS-client-certificate topology. Neither mechanism protects a fully compromised client that loses both token and key.

:::deep
A service mesh can automate issuance, rotation, and transport policy, but it is not “security with no code or operations.”

Define trust domains, namespace/service authorization, certificate lifetime, clock-skew behavior, CA/root rotation, revocation/compromise response, telemetry, and fail-open/fail-closed behavior.

Test that plaintext bypass paths are closed.

Use mTLS where the threat model and platform justify it; “every request must use a mesh” is not a universal architecture rule. It adds proxies or library integration, control-plane dependencies, latency/resource cost, and another policy layer.

Cloud workload federation or signed workload tokens may fit some boundaries better.

Keep service identity and end-user delegation separate. An mTLS peer may be `booking-service`, while a scoped token says it is acting for user U on booking B. Authorization should evaluate both when both matter.
:::

items.q: How should OWASP Top 10:2025 and API Security Top 10:2023 shape backend controls?
items.a:
Treat both lists as [[o:awareness and threat-modelling inputs]], not a compliance checklist. OWASP Top 10:2025 emphasizes broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply-chain failures, cryptographic/injection/insecure-design/authentication failures, integrity, logging/alerting, and mishandled exceptional conditions. API Security Top 10:2023 adds API-specific focus such as object/function/property authorization, resource consumption, sensitive business flows, SSRF, inventory, and unsafe consumption of upstream APIs.
RiskEngineering controls
injection / XSS / CSRFparameter binding; context-aware output encoding and CSP; SameSite plus CSRF tokens for cookie-authenticated writes
BOLA/IDOR and function/property authorizationserver-side tenant, object, field, and action checks on every path; deny by default; test negative cases
resource and sensitive-flow abusepayload/page limits, deadlines, quotas, bot/fraud controls, idempotency, and cost-aware admission
SSRF / unsafe upstream APIsdestination allowlists, safe URL parsing, egress controls, response validation, timeouts,
and no blind redirect/credential forwarding
supply chain and integritylocked dependencies, SCA, SBOM, provenance, signed artifacts, isolated builds, and
signature/policy verification at deploy
:::deep Mass assignment is prevented by explicit input DTOs/allowlists, not by hiding fields in the UI. Error paths need the same authorization and data-minimization rules as success paths: fail closed where correctness/security requires it, return stable problem details, and avoid stack traces or secrets in responses. Build a security test matrix from assets and abuse cases: cross-tenant IDs, role downgrade, hidden fields, large/deep payloads, race/replay, webhook SSRF, partner schema surprises, dependency compromise, key rotation, and unavailable policy/identity services. Run SAST/SCA/secret scanning early, DAST and authorization tests against a deployed system, then verify audit/alert signals through incident exercises. WAF and rate limiting are defense in depth, not substitutes for resource-level authorization, safe code, or business-flow anti-automation. :::

items.q: How do you manage secrets properly?
How do you protect auth endpoints from brute-force/credential stuffing?
items.a:
- rate limit by IP + by account
- exponential backoff/temporary lockout; CAPTCHA after N failed attempts
- detect anomalies (login from an unusual location)
- store passwords with a slow, salted hash function ([[g:bcrypt/argon2/scrypt]]), [[r:never plain MD5/SHA]]
- MFA for sensitive operations
- [[o:don't reveal 'whether the user exists']] through error messages

:::deep
- rate limit + lockout by IP *and* by account (defends against credential stuffing across many IPs against one account, & brute-force against one account from one IP); exponential backoff; CAPTCHA past a threshold; anomaly detection (unfamiliar location/device → step-up MFA)
- [[g:argon2id]] (recommended) / bcrypt / scrypt — NEVER plain MD5/SHA (fast, easy to brute-force on GPUs); don't leak 'user exists' via errors/timing (timing-safe)

Fintech/OTA: require phishing-resistant or step-up MFA where transaction risk, regulation and recovery policy demand it; prefer passkeys/WebAuthn where supported, and treat device/location signals as risk inputs rather than identity proof.

[[r:Pitfall]]: lockout too aggressive → DoS against the real user (an attacker locks out the victim's account) → use CAPTCHA instead of a hard lockout, or lock by IP+account combined.
:::

items.q: RBAC vs ABAC — which authorization model should you choose?
items.a:
RBACABAC
Basisroles (admin, teller)attributes (user, resource, context, time)
Prossimple, easy to manage/auditflexible for complex rules
Consrole explosion as rules get complexharder to debug/audit
Many systems combine both: RBAC as the base + ABAC for fine-grained rules. :::deep - ABAC example: 'an agent may only approve bookings below their branch's limit during working hours' - engines: OPA/Rego, Cedar for policy-as-code decoupled from business logic OTA: RBAC for customer/agent/admin; ABAC for 'agent from airline X only sees airline X's bookings', 'refunds above a threshold need higher-level approval'. [[o:Check permissions server-side]] (gateway + service), never trust the client; log every sensitive authorization decision (audit). :::

items.q: API key vs OAuth token — when do you use which?
items.a:
API keyOAuth token
Identifiesan application/partnera user/scope
Granularitylowhigh (scope)
Lifetimestatic, long-livedshort-lived, revocable
Good forpartner server-to-serveracting on behalf of a user
:::deep - [[b:API key]]: a secret string identifying an application/partner (not a user), used alongside an IP allowlist + rate limit/quota. [[r:Risk]]: static, long-lived, once leaked it stays usable indefinitely → needs rotation + a restricted scope - [[b:OAuth token]]: authorization scoped to a user/scope, short-lived, revocable OTA/fintech: B2C → OAuth/OIDC; internal services → mTLS + client-credentials; B2B partners → API key + mTLS + quota, or client-credentials with scope. Managing API keys: [[g:hash them at rest]] (like a password), use a prefix for identification, rotate without downtime (two keys active simultaneously during rotation), audit. [[r:Never embed an API key in a client/mobile app]] (too easy to extract). :::

items.q: What is Keycloak, and what are realms, clients and its core endpoints?
items.a:
Keycloak is an [[g:open-source identity provider]] (CNCF incubating since 2023) implementing OAuth 2.x, OIDC and SAML 2.0. It plays the [[o:authorization server]] role from (13-security-oauth2.oauth2-oidc.q1) so you do not build login, MFA, federation and token issuance yourself. **The object model, from the outside in:**
ConceptWhat it isGotcha
realmAn isolated tenant: its own users, roles, clients and [[o:signing keys]]Cross-realm token trust does not exist. master is for administering Keycloak — never put application users there
clientOne application asking for tokenspublic (SPA/mobile, no secret, PKCE required) vs confidential (backend, has a secret)
client scopeReusable bundle of claims/roles added to a tokenDefault scopes apply silently; optional ones only when requested
realm role / client roleRealm-wide vs per-client authorityThey land in *different* token claims — see (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q3)
identity providerUpstream federation (Google, Azure AD, LDAP)Keycloak still mints its own token; the upstream one is not what your API sees
**Every endpoint is advertised by discovery** — never hardcode paths: 
// one document tells you every other URL
GET /realms/{realm}/.well-known/openid-configuration
//
authorization_endpoint  /realms/{r}/protocol/openid-connect/auth
token_endpoint          /realms/{r}/protocol/openid-connect/token
jwks_uri                /realms/{r}/protocol/openid-connect/certs
end_session_endpoint    /realms/{r}/protocol/openid-connect/logout
introspection_endpoint  /realms/{r}/protocol/openid-connect/token/introspect
:::tip Interview framing Say what Keycloak *replaces*: it is the authorization server, so your services keep only token *validation* — the resource-server half. That split is the whole reason to adopt it. ::: :::deep - **`issuer` must match exactly**, character for character, including scheme, port and any trailing path. A Keycloak behind a reverse proxy that rewrites the host mints tokens whose `iss` your service then rejects — fix it with `KC_HOSTNAME` plus `--proxy-headers=xforwarded`, not by loosening validation. - Keycloak is stateful: it needs a real database ([[r:not the dev-mode H2]]) and, for a cluster, an Infinispan cache for sessions. Run `start` and not `start-dev` in production — the latter disables HTTPS requirements and uses an in-memory store. - The legacy `keycloak-spring-boot-starter` and its adapters are [[r:end-of-life]]. New services must use plain Spring Security OAuth2 resource server (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q2); there is nothing Keycloak-specific left on the resource-server side. - Realm config belongs in version control. Export it and import declaratively (`kc.sh import`, or the Keycloak Operator's `KeycloakRealmImport`) so the IdP is reproducible rather than a hand-clicked snowflake. :::

items.q: How does a Spring Boot service validate a Keycloak token, and what must you verify?
items.a:
Your service is a [[g:resource server]]: it never talks to Keycloak per request. It fetches the [[o:JWKS]] once, caches the public keys, and verifies signatures locally — the mechanism from (13-security-oauth2.jwt-tokens.q1). **The whole configuration is one property:** 
# issuer-uri alone is enough — Spring reads discovery and finds the JWKS
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: \
  https://kc.example.com/realms/fintech
#
# it validates: signature, exp, nbf, and iss — but NOT audience
**`aud` is not checked by default, and that is the trap.** Any token from the same realm — including one minted for a completely different client — verifies fine. Add the check explicitly: 
@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(OAuth2ResourceServerProperties p) {
    String issuer = p.getJwt().getIssuerUri();
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);
    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
        JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer),      // sig, exp, iss
        new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>(               // the missing one
            "aud", aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("orders-api"))));
    return decoder;
}
Getting `aud` into the token at all takes a Keycloak-side [[o:audience mapper]] on the client — by default Keycloak puts the client only in `azp`, so `aud` may be absent entirely. :::warn Never trust these Do not authorize on `preferred_username` or `email` — both are mutable and `email` need not be verified. Bind rows to the [[r:immutable `sub`]], exactly as the local app does with the Google token (see the security model in `CLAUDE.md`). ::: :::deep - **JWKS caching and key rotation.** Spring refreshes the key set when it sees an unknown `kid`, with a rate limit (default 5 minutes) so a bad token cannot turn into a JWKS stampede. Rotate keys in Keycloak *before* retiring the old one — it keeps serving both so in-flight tokens stay valid. - **Local verification means revocation is not immediate** — the same trade-off as (13-security-oauth2.jwt-tokens.q2). - Usual answer: short access-token lifetimes (1–5 min) plus refresh-token rotation. - `introspect` gives instant revocation, at the cost of a network hop and a hard Keycloak dependency on every request. - **`realm_access` is not a Spring authority.** Spring reads `scope`/`scp` by default, so `hasRole('ADMIN')` fails silently until you supply a converter (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q3). - Keycloak must be reachable at startup only if you build the decoder eagerly; `JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation` fetches discovery immediately, which makes a cold Keycloak a boot failure. Use `NimbusJwtDecoder.withJwkSetUri(...)` for lazy fetching when boot ordering matters. :::

items.q: Where do Keycloak roles land in the token, and how do you map them to Spring authorities?
items.a:
Keycloak writes roles into [[o:nested claims]] that Spring Security does not read, so a fresh integration authenticates correctly and then fails every authorization check. **What is actually in the token:** 
{
  "sub": "8f14e45f-…",           // the only stable user id
  "azp": "orders-web",           // which client asked
  "realm_access": { "roles": ["admin", "teller"] },
  "resource_access": {              // per-client roles
    "orders-api": { "roles": ["orders:write"] }
  },
  "scope": "openid profile email"   // <-- Spring reads ONLY this
}
**The converter that bridges the gap:** 
static Collection<GrantedAuthority> authorities(Jwt jwt) {
    Map<String,Object> realm = jwt.getClaim("realm_access");
    if (realm == null) return List.of();
    var roles = (Collection<String>) realm.getOrDefault("roles", List.of());
    return roles.stream()
        // hasRole('ADMIN') looks for the ROLE_ prefix; omit it and
        // only hasAuthority('admin') works — a classic silent 403
        .<GrantedAuthority>map(r -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r.toUpperCase()))
        .toList();
}
DecisionUse
Authority spanning every servicerealm_access — a realm role
Permission meaningful to one API onlyresource_access — a client role, so orders:write cannot leak authority into the payments service
What the *client app* may ask for, not what the user isscope — delegation, not identity
:::deep - **Composite roles** expand at token-mint time, so `manager` containing `teller` arrives as both. Convenient, and the reason tokens quietly grow — a user in many groups can push the JWT past an 8 KB proxy header limit. Keep coarse roles in the token and resolve fine-grained permissions service-side. - **Group membership is not in the token by default.** Add a group-membership mapper if you need it, but prefer mapping groups to roles: groups are an organisational structure, roles are the authorization contract. - **`scope` vs role is a real interview distinction:** [[g:scope is what the client may request]], [[o:role is what the user is]]. - `scope=openid` with `realm_access.roles=[admin]` = an admin using an app granted only identity access. - Both limits apply, and the effective permission is the intersection. - Prefer `@PreAuthorize` on the method over URL-pattern matching for anything non-trivial; the model is RBAC/ABAC from (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q6), and Keycloak only supplies the attributes. :::

items.q: How do services call each other with Keycloak, and what is token exchange for?
items.a:
Two different problems, two different grants — conflating them is a common design error. **Service acting as itself → `client_credentials`.** There is no user; the token's `sub` is the service account: 
POST /realms/fintech/protocol/openid-connect/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
//
grant_type=client_credentials
&client_id=batch-poster&client_secret=…
**Service acting on behalf of a user → [[o:token exchange]]** (RFC 8693). The gateway holds the user's token; the downstream service needs one scoped to itself but still carrying the user's identity: 
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=<the caller's access token>
&audience=ledger-api          // mint for this service
// result: a NEW token, aud=ledger-api, sub still the original user
ApproachWhen it is rightCost
Forward the same tokenTrusted internal mesh, one audience[[r:Any hop can replay it anywhere]] — audience is meaningless
Token exchangeCrossing a trust boundary while keeping user identityA Keycloak round-trip per hop (cache it for the token's lifetime)
client_credentialsBatch jobs, cron, no user involvedLoses user identity — audit logs show only the service
:::warn Do not forward a user token indefinitely A token minted for `orders-api` and forwarded through four services can be replayed by any of them against any service in the realm. Set a real `audience` and validate it (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q2) — that is what makes the boundary mean something. ::: :::deep - **Token exchange is opt-in per client**, gated by fine-grained admin permissions: the exchanging client needs explicit authority over the target audience. - It has moved between "preview" and supported across versions — [[o:check the feature flags for the version you actually run]] rather than assuming. - For pure machine-to-machine inside a cluster, [[g:mTLS]] (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q2) may replace tokens entirely: the identity is the certificate and there is nothing to steal or replay. Use tokens when you need *user* identity to travel; use mTLS when you need *service* identity. - Bind the token to the client that holds it where the stakes justify it: mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705) or DPoP make a stolen bearer token useless elsewhere. - Cache service tokens and refresh before `exp`, honouring `expires_in`. A service that requests a fresh token per outbound call turns Keycloak into the bottleneck for the entire system. :::

items.q: What breaks when you run Keycloak in production?
items.a:
Keycloak is not a stateless sidecar — it is a [[r:database-backed, clustered, single point of failure for every login]]. The failure modes are operational, not conceptual.
FailureCauseFix
invalid_token, issuer mismatchProxy rewrites the host; iss no longer matches what services expectKC_HOSTNAME + --proxy-headers=xforwarded; never "fix" it by skipping validation
Random logouts in a clusterSessions live in Infinispan; a node dies with the only copyDistributed cache with owners > 1, sticky sessions at the LB
Slow logins under loadEvery login writes to the DB; connection pool exhaustedSize the pool, watch DB latency — Keycloak is as fast as its database
Token verification stalls everywhereKeycloak down and services fetch JWKS per requestCache the JWKS (default in Spring); verification must survive a Keycloak outage
Upgrade breaks the realmDB schema migrates in place, and it is one-wayBack up the DB, test the upgrade on a copy, pin the image tag
**The thing to say out loud:** if Keycloak is down, [[g:existing tokens keep working]] (local verification) but [[r:nobody can log in or refresh]]. That asymmetry decides your token lifetimes — long enough to ride out a restart, short enough that revocation means something. :::tip Capacity reality Login is expensive (password hashing is deliberately slow — Argon2 by default in recent versions), token *verification* is free because it happens in your service. Size Keycloak for the login and refresh rate, not for request throughput. ::: :::deep - **Run it HA, and treat the DB as the tier that matters:** at least two replicas, a real Postgres/MySQL with backups, PodDisruptionBudget, and readiness on `/health/ready` (management port 9000 in recent versions). - The Keycloak Operator handles most of this on Kubernetes (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.docker-kubernetes.q6). - **Blast radius.** One realm for every application means one bad realm export takes down every login. Separate tenants into separate realms; keep `master` for administration only. - **Observability** — alert on login failure rate (credential stuffing, see (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q5)), token endpoint p99, DB pool saturation, and Infinispan cluster size. - Keycloak exposes Micrometer metrics; feed them into the same stack as (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q1). - **Do not fork Keycloak to add a feature.** Use its extension points (SPIs, custom authenticators, event listeners) — a forked IdP is unupgradable, and upgrades are how you get security fixes. :::

items.q: Keycloak vs a managed IdP vs rolling your own — how do you argue the choice?
items.a:
Interviewers ask this to hear whether you can weigh [[o:operational cost against control]] instead of naming a favourite.
Keycloak (self-hosted)Managed (Auth0/Cognito/Entra)Build it yourself
Cost shapeInfra + your ops time; flat as users growPer-MAU — cheap early, painful at scaleCheapest to start, most expensive to keep
Data residency[[g:You hold the user data]] — often the deciding factor in fintechThird party holds it; check the jurisdictionYou hold it, including the breach
You now operateA clustered stateful service + DB (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q5)NothingPassword hashing, MFA, token revocation, federation, and every CVE
CustomisationDeep — SPIs, custom flows, own login themeBounded by the vendorUnlimited, and entirely your problem
Lock-inLow: standard OIDC, exportable realmReal: proprietary rules and user storeNone
**The defensible position:** [[r:never build your own]] for authentication — it is the least differentiating, highest-blast-radius code you could write. - Choose **managed** when the team is small and data residency permits. - Choose **Keycloak** when residency, per-user cost, or protocol control decide it. Both keep you on standard OIDC, so the resource-server code in (13-security-oauth2.keycloak-in-practice.q2) is [[g:unchanged either way]] — which is exactly why the decision is reversible. :::deep - The migration path is the point worth making: because both speak OIDC, switching IdP changes an `issuer-uri` and a role-claim converter, not your services. What does *not* migrate cleanly is password hashes (formats differ — usually a rehash-on-next-login shim) and the vendor-specific rules engine. - Keycloak is [[o:Apache 2.0 with no open-core split]], so there is no feature paywall; the cost is the operations. That matters when comparing against products whose SSO or audit-log tier is priced separately. - If you take Keycloak for its features but not its operations, hosted Keycloak (Red Hat build of Keycloak, or a managed provider) is the middle path and a good answer to "what if we lack an ops team?". - Whatever you choose, the [[g:security model stays yours]]: `aud` validation, immutable `sub` as the user key, short token lifetimes, and authorization decided in your service. An IdP outsources authentication, never authorization. :::

items.q: Injection is more than SQL. Where does untrusted input still reach an interpreter in a modern Spring service?
items.a:
Parameter binding solved the textbook case and moved the problem elsewhere. Injection survives everywhere a string is [[r:assembled]] rather than bound.
SurfaceThe unsafe shapeThe fix
JPQL / native SQLstring concatenation into the querybind parameters; never concatenate values
Dynamic ORDER BY / table nameidentifiers cannot be bound, so people concatenateallowlist of column names, map input to constants
MongoDB filtersa raw map from the request body becomes the querybind typed fields; reject `$` operators from clients
Shell / process`Runtime.exec("sh -c " + arg)`pass an argument array, no shell
Logsuser text written straight into the log linestructured fields, encode newlines
Templates / expressionsuser string evaluated as SpEL or a templatenever evaluate user input as an expression
// unsafe: sort is a request parameter concatenated into JPQL
var q = em.createQuery("select o from Order o order by o." + sort);
//
// safe: identifiers come from a closed set the code owns
private static final Map<String, String> SORTS =
        Map.of("created", "createdAt", "total", "totalAmount");
var column = SORTS.getOrDefault(sort, "createdAt");   // unknown input degrades, never injects
:::tip The rule that generalises Data is bound, structure is chosen from a set you control. If input decides *structure* — a column, a table, an operator, a class name — it must be mapped through an allowlist. ::: :::deep - [[o:log injection]] is underrated: a newline in a username lets an attacker forge log lines and poison the incident timeline you will trust later (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). - second-order injection stores the payload safely and interpolates it later in a report or admin query. The dangerous moment is the read, not the write. - ORMs are not immunity: `@Query` with concatenation, native queries, `Specification` built from raw strings and JPQL `LIKE` patterns are all reachable. - validation is not the control here, it is defence in depth. Reject obviously wrong input early (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q8), then still bind properly. - for MongoDB, an untyped `Map` from the body can smuggle `{"$ne": null}` into a filter and turn an equality check into "match anything" (07-sql-nosql-db-engines.engine-by-engine.q4). :::

items.q: A user sets their own role by adding one field to the request body. How does mass assignment happen and how is it closed?
items.a:
Mass assignment is what happens when the request body is bound straight onto a persistent object. The client controls every field the class exposes, including the ones no form ever shows. 
// the entity has fields the client must never set
@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
User update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody User body) {   // entity as the API type
    body.setId(id);
    return users.save(body);        // role, status, credit, verified — all writable
}
//
// the DTO is the contract: it can only carry what the caller is allowed to change
record UpdateProfile(@NotBlank String displayName, @Email String email) { }
//
@PutMapping("/users/{id}")
UserView update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody @Valid UpdateProfile in) {
    var user = users.findOwned(id, currentUser());   // authorisation, not just authentication
    user.rename(in.displayName());
    return UserView.of(user);
}
**Three defences, in order of strength:** - [[g:a dedicated DTO per operation]] — the type system makes the extra field impossible, not merely rejected - [[g:explicit mapping]] into the domain object, so adding an entity field never silently widens the API - [[g:reject unknown properties]] (`FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES`) so a renamed or dropped field fails loudly instead of being ignored :::warn Response side has the same bug Serialising the entity back leaks `passwordHash`, internal flags and the whole object graph. A view model is not ceremony; it is the outbound half of the same control. ::: :::deep - this is [[r:broken object property level authorisation]] in the API Security Top 10 — the same family as IDOR, one level down: not "which object" but "which field of it" (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q3). - the field does not have to exist today. Adding `isAdmin` to an entity six months later silently turns a safe endpoint into a privilege escalation. - separating the domain model from the JPA entity removes the temptation entirely, and pays for itself in other ways too (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2). - `@JsonIgnore` and `setDisallowedFields` work but are [[o:denylists]]: they protect the fields somebody remembered. The DTO is an allowlist by construction. - test it as a security case: post a body containing `role` and assert the stored role is unchanged. That test outlives every reviewer's memory (26-testing-strategy.what-a-test-is-for.q1). :::

items.q: Which parsing and deserialization features turn "just reading input" into remote code execution or a denial of service?
items.a:
Every parser is an interpreter with a large feature set. The dangerous ones let the *document* decide which code runs or how much memory is allocated.
FeatureWhat an attacker getsControl
Java native `Serializable`gadget chains → code execution on readObjectnever accept it from outside; use JSON with a schema
Polymorphic typing by class nameinstantiates classes you never intendedno default typing; bind a sealed set of subtypes
XML external entities (XXE)reads local files, reaches internal hostsdisable DTDs and external entities on every factory
Deeply nested or huge JSONstack overflow, heap exhaustionsize limits, depth limits, streaming parse
Compressed uploadszip bomb: 1 MB expands to 10 GBcap the decompressed size while expanding
Catastrophic regexone request pins a CPU corebounded patterns, no user-supplied regex
// polymorphic JSON, done safely: the set of types is closed and named by the code
@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, property = "kind")
@JsonSubTypes({ @Type(value = CardPayment.class, name = "card"),
              @Type(value = BankTransfer.class, name = "bank") })
sealed interface PaymentInstruction permits CardPayment, BankTransfer { }
**For uploads, validate before you trust the name:** - decide the type from content, not from the extension or the client's `Content-Type` - store outside the web root with a generated name; never execute or serve it back inline - cap size at the edge and again while decompressing, and scan when the file will be shared with others :::warn A file upload is untrusted input that persists It is stored, retrieved, and often rendered later by a different component with different assumptions. That later component is where the exploit lands. ::: :::deep - the [[r:root cause]] is trusting the document to choose behaviour. Ask of every parser: can the input decide which class is created, which file is read, or how much memory is allocated? - responses matter too: serve user files from a separate origin with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy`, so a stored HTML file cannot execute in your domain. - limits belong at the edge as well as in code — the proxy rejects a 2 GB body long before the JVM tries to buffer it (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.web-server-networking-observability.q1). - log and alert on [[o:parse failures at volume]]: a sudden burst of malformed payloads is usually somebody probing, not a broken client. - fuzz the parsing layer of anything that accepts third-party data; it is one of the few places where random input finds real bugs cheaply (26-testing-strategy.what-a-test-is-for.q4). :::

items.q: Your service fetches a URL the user supplied. What is the full SSRF blast radius and what actually stops it?
items.a:
SSRF turns your service into the attacker's proxy: it already sits inside the network, already holds credentials, and is already trusted by everything around it. **Typical entry points:** avatar-from-URL, webhook registration, PDF or link preview generation, XML with external entities, an import job that takes a file URL, and any "callback URL" field. 
attacker → POST /import {"url": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/…"}
              → your pod fetches it with its own identity
              → response body returned to the attacker
ControlStrengthWhy it fails alone
Blocking `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`weak`0.0.0.0`, IPv6, decimal and octal forms, DNS names that resolve inward
Allowlist of hostsstrongonly workable when destinations are known
Resolve then validate the IPstrongmust re-check after redirects and pin the resolved address
Egress firewall / proxystrongestthe one control that survives a code mistake
Disable redirects, cap size and timesupportinglimits the damage rather than preventing it
:::tip What makes SSRF different from other input bugs Validating the string is not enough, because DNS can answer differently the second time. Validate the [[g:resolved address]] and then connect to that address, not to the name again. ::: :::deep - the cloud metadata endpoint is the classic prize; it hands out instance credentials. Enforce the hardened metadata service and give the workload the narrowest role it can do its job with (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.ci-cd-2026-best-practices.q5). - internal services usually have [[r:no authentication]] because "they are internal". SSRF is exactly the assumption breaker, which is why service-to-service auth belongs everywhere (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q2). - blind SSRF still works without a response body: timing and DNS lookups leak whether a host exists, which is enough to map a network. - treat outbound fetches as a privileged operation: run them from a component with its own restricted egress, not from the service holding your database credentials. - webhooks make you the caller by design, so the same controls apply to every delivery attempt, including retries (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q1). :::

items.q: Storage is encrypted, so the data is safe. Which attacks does that actually stop, and which does it not?
items.a:
Disk-level encryption protects the disk. Almost every incident that matters reaches the data through the application, which sees plaintext by design.
LayerStopsDoes not stop
Full-disk / volumea stolen or discarded diskany authenticated query, SQL injection, a leaked dump
Database TDEreading data files or backups directlya DBA, a compromised app, `SELECT *`
Field-level (app encrypts)DBA access, dumps, most injectionsthe service itself once it is compromised
Tokenisation / vaultthe value never enters your systemabuse of the token where it is accepted
Hashing (passwords)reversal after a breachweak passwords, credential stuffing
**Start from a data classification, not from a technology:** - public, internal, personal, and regulated (payment, health, government id) - for each class: who may read it, how long it is kept, and where it may be copied - the strongest control is [[g:not storing it]] — a field nobody stores cannot leak :::warn "Encrypted at rest" is a compliance sentence, not a threat model Say which attacker it stops. If the answer is "somebody who steals the physical disk", it is true and rarely the attacker you have. ::: :::deep - field-level encryption has to answer the [[o:query problem]] first: an encrypted column cannot be searched or ranged over. A blind index (a keyed hash of the normalised value) buys equality lookups only, and leaks equality. - key management is the real work: a key in the same database is decoration. Use a KMS, keep keys per environment, and rotate with a key id stored next to the ciphertext so old rows stay readable. - passwords are not encrypted, they are hashed with a memory-hard function — that distinction still separates engineers in interviews (13-security-oauth2.designing-the-auth-system.q5). - backups and non-production copies inherit the classification. A staging database restored from production is a production data breach waiting for a weaker password. - pick the layer by threat: TDE for lost media and auditors, field-level for insiders and dumps, tokenisation to remove the data from scope entirely. :::

items.q: Where does sensitive data actually leak in a well-built system, and how do you close those paths?
items.a:
Breaches through the front door make the news; the routine leaks are internal copies nobody classified.
PathWhat escapesControl
Logsrequest bodies, tokens, card numbers, full stack tracesstructured fields with an allowlist, never log whole payloads
Traces and metricsidentifiers as span attributes or labelsallowlisted baggage, no PII in labels
Error responsesinternal messages, SQL fragments, hostnamesa stable error contract, detail behind a trace id
Support and admin screensfull records to anyone with the rolemask by default, reveal on justified action, log the reveal
Exports and reportseverything, downloaded to a laptopscoped columns, expiring links, audit each export
Non-production copiesthe whole database, weakly guardedanonymise or synthesise on the way out of production
Third-party toolswhatever the SDK collects by defaultreview defaults, scrub before send
// masking belongs in the type, not in each log statement
record Pan(String value) {
    public String toString() { return "****" + value.substring(value.length() - 4); }
}
:::tip The design move that scales Wrap sensitive values in their own type whose `toString` is already masked. Then a careless log line, an exception message and a debugger all show the masked form by default. ::: :::deep - [[r:the most common leak is an exception]]: a message containing the offending value, serialised into an error response or shipped to an aggregator. Log the trace id, keep detail server-side (17-rest-api-design.contracts-errors-lifecycle.q2). - "temporary" debug logging is the second: it is added during an incident, survives the fix, and quietly writes card numbers for months. - anonymisation is harder than masking. A dataset with a birth date, a postcode and a gender is usually re-identifiable; sampling and generalising beats replacing names. - treat the [[o:log pipeline as a data store]] with its own retention, access control and audit. It frequently holds more sensitive data than the database does (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). - add a CI check for the obvious patterns — card-like digit runs and `Authorization:` in log statements — because review misses them at 2am. :::

items.q: How do retention, deletion requests and an immutable audit trail coexist when the two requirements contradict each other?
items.a:
"Delete everything about me" and "keep an immutable financial record" are both real obligations. The resolution is to separate the identity from the transaction.
DataObligationDesign
Identity and contact detailserasable on requestone owning service, referenced by id elsewhere
Financial and tax recordsretain for yearskeep the amounts and the id, drop the personal fields
Security audit trailtamper-evident, retainedappend-only, actor as a stable id, not a name
Behavioural and analytics dataminimise and expireaggregate early, keep no raw identifiers
**What makes erasure achievable at all:** - personal data lives in [[g:one place]] and everything else stores a reference, so deletion is one operation instead of a manhunt - [[g:crypto-shredding]] for stores you cannot rewrite: encrypt per subject and destroy that subject's key, which renders backups and archives unreadable without rewriting them - an inventory of copies: search index, cache, data warehouse, exports, partner systems, backups — a deletion that misses these is not a deletion :::warn Backups are the requirement everyone forgets You cannot rewrite last month's backup. Either commit to a retention window after which backups age out, or make the data unreadable by destroying its key. ::: :::deep - an audit trail answers "who did what to which record, and when" — including [[o:reads of sensitive data]], which is what regulators ask for first and what most systems cannot answer at all. - append-only plus a hash chain gives tamper evidence cheaply: each entry carries a hash of the previous one, so silent edits become detectable. - separate the audit trail from application logs. Logs are operational, rotate quickly and can be edited; audit records are evidence with their own retention (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). - a ledger keeps corrections as new entries rather than updates, which is the same discipline that makes financial records reconstructable (09-distributed-tx-fintech.correctness-where-money-is-involved.q3). - write the retention rule as code — a scheduled job with its own tests — rather than a paragraph in a policy document nobody executes. :::

items.q: Most of your running code came from other people. How do you keep dependencies and images from becoming the breach?
items.a:
A typical service ships a few thousand lines of your code on top of hundreds of megabytes of other people's. Supply chain work is about knowing what you ship and being able to replace it quickly. **The practices that matter, in order of payoff:** - [[g:know what is in there]] — generate an SBOM at build time and keep it with the artifact, so answering "are we affected by this CVE?" takes minutes rather than a week - [[g:scan continuously, not at release]] — a dependency that was clean at build becomes vulnerable the day an advisory is published - [[g:upgrade on a cadence]] — small, frequent updates are how you stay able to patch fast; a two-year-old framework turns an urgent fix into a migration project - [[g:pin and verify]] — exact versions and digests, lockfiles committed, images pinned by digest so a moved tag cannot swap your base layer
SurfaceWhat to check
Application dependenciesdirect and transitive CVEs, licence, abandoned projects
Base imageOS package CVEs, size, non-root user, distroless where possible
Build pipelinewho can trigger it, what secrets it can read, provenance of artifacts
Plugins and actionsthird-party CI steps run with your credentials
:::tip The question that reframes the work Not "do we have vulnerabilities?" — you do. It is "how long does it take us to ship a patched build?" Everything else follows from that number. ::: :::deep - triage by [[o:reachability]], not by CVSS alone: a critical rating in a code path you never call is lower priority than a medium one on your request path. Blind severity queues cause alert fatigue and then get ignored. - the build pipeline is production. It holds credentials for every environment, so a compromised CI step is a compromised deployment (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.ci-cd-2026-best-practices.q4). - pin third-party CI actions to a commit digest; tags are mutable and have been repointed to malicious code in real incidents. - keep one artifact promoted through environments rather than rebuilding per stage, so what you scanned is exactly what you run (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.ci-cd-2026-best-practices.q1). - transitive dependencies are the majority of the risk and the hardest to reason about; dependency management that reports the resolved graph is worth more than a scanner nobody reads (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q3). :::
